{"id": "2:228/q29", "question": "What is the 'degree' men have?", "turns_on": "Whether it names a specific advantage, the duties that accompany authority, an exhortation to generosity, or a broad preference.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q29/p1", "position": "A broad advantage in rights, authority and allotted responsibilities.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others name governance, obedience, inheritance, jihad and legal privileges. Qadi and Ibn Atiyya say the views can combine; Razi says greater advantage makes abuse more blameworthy."}, {"id": "2:228/q29/p2", "position": "The duty to be generous, waive some claims and fulfill women's due.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's account is preferred by Tabari and praised by Ibn Atiyya; it reads the degree after the rights clause as an exhortation to forbearance."}, {"id": "2:228/q29/p3", "position": "Men's dowry, maintenance, protection and care.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas, Zajjaj, Abu Ishaq, Razi and others say spouses share enjoyment but husbands bear extra expense; 4:34 is cited."}, {"id": "2:228/q29/p4", "position": "Control over divorce, revocation and particular legal asymmetries.", "reasons": "Sha'bi adds dowry and liʿān, Abu Malik names unilateral divorce, and other reports name testimony, polygyny, blood money or leadership."}, {"id": "2:228/q29/p5", "position": "Jihad, inheritance, strength, intellect or religious obligations.", "reasons": "Mujahid cites jihad and inheritance, Qatada jihad, while unattributed reports name intellect and bodily strength. Kuranyolu disputes using a hadith to claim women are generally inferior in intellect."}, {"id": "2:228/q29/p6", "position": "A beard.", "reasons": "Humayd's gloss is transmitted, but Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi reject it as unsupported by the wording or meaning."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q30", "question": "What does daraja mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q30/p1", "position": "A rank, station or step of ascent.", "reasons": "Majaz, Jishumi, Razi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Wahidi and Alusi connect it to progressing by stages or a road's steps; related rajul forms are tied to strength."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q31", "question": "What does the closing pair 'Mighty, Wise' teach?", "turns_on": "Whether might is emphasized as vengeance or blessing.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q31/p1", "position": "God can punish violations and legislates these duties wisely.", "reasons": "Tabari links the closing to commands from 2:221 onward; Zajjaj, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Alusi and others stress irresistible rule and wisdom in law."}, {"id": "2:228/q31/p2", "position": "Might here can mean might in blessing.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports Hasan and Qatada for blessing, beside Abu al-Aliya and Rabi' for vengeance."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q32", "question": "What occasion or historical practice is reported behind the verse?", "turns_on": "Different reports identify different people or prior practices.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q32/p1", "position": "Asmāʾ bint Yazīd was the first divorcee for whom a waiting period was revealed.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Kathir, Durr and Tabataba'i report her divorce when no term existed; Ibn Kathir calls the chain strange."}, {"id": "2:228/q32/p2", "position": "An Ismāʿīl or Mālik of Ghifār or the Anṣār reclaimed a pregnant wife who later died with her child.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Jishumi give variants of the man and wife and a later death; Durr reports the Ghifar version."}, {"id": "2:228/q32/p3", "position": "Women concealed pregnancy to assign children to later husbands.", "reasons": "Qatada and other reports describe the pre-Islamic practice as prompting the ban."}, {"id": "2:228/q32/p4", "position": "Husbands repeatedly divorced and revoked near the term's end to harm wives.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Jishumi, Tabarsi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others describe the abusive cycle."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q33", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from the waiting and return?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q33/p1", "position": "The interval figures God's patience with servants and the possibility of repentance.", "reasons": "Bursevi says God delays turning away so love and repentance may return, and calls seekers to remain at His threshold; Study Quran applies reciprocal rights to soul and spirit."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q34", "question": "What broader social setting is used to explain the reciprocal-rights clause?", "turns_on": "How women's prior treatment and natural or social roles bear on the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q34/p1", "position": "Earlier societies often denied women independent rights; Islam restored their human standing.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i surveys China, India, Egypt, Iran, Greece, Rome and pre-Islamic Arabia, then invokes 49:13, 3:195 and other verses for equal moral accountability and independent property. Kuranyolu cites Umar's recollection of change."}, {"id": "2:228/q34/p2", "position": "Equal human worth coexists with differing family roles and responsibilities.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i argues from fitra, procreation, maintenance, inheritance and social capacity; Kuranyolu stresses balance and role-based duties while rejecting lesser humanity or inherent intellectual inferiority."}, {"id": "2:228/q34/p3", "position": "The verse's rights can adapt in details governed by maʿrūf.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu cites the Prophet's allocation of household and outside tasks to Fatima and Ali, and jurists who regard it as contingent rather than permanent."}]}
{"id": "2:228/q35", "question": "What ancillary linguistic or report material appears in sources citing this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:228/q35/p1", "position": "Some cited sections discuss related Arabic grammar, Qur'anic recitation, parables, virtues or historical material beyond this verse.", "reasons": "Sibawayh surveys plural and assimilation patterns; Jurjani discusses parable and repetition; Ibn Kathir cites virtues and comparisons; al-Itqan discusses Qur'an collectors and general language principles. These are retained as source context."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q01", "question": "What fear does the conditional describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the implied threat is restricted to enemies, extends to other dangers, or concerns loss of prayer time.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q01/p1", "position": "Fear of an enemy or combatant.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Muqatil, Wahidi and Razi's report of Wahidi identify the omitted object as enemy; Wahidi says the context supplies it. Study Quran adds battle or persecution."}, {"id": "2:239/q01/p2", "position": "Fear from an enemy or any other danger.", "reasons": "Tabari, Thalabi, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Abu Hayyan and others cite pursuit, predator, attacking camel, fire or flood; Razi argues from the verse's general wording and the harm-prevention rationale. Biqai also mentions a creditor one may lawfully flee."}, {"id": "2:239/q01/p3", "position": "Fear that the prayer time will end before fighting ceases.", "reasons": "Razi reports this third reading and says it stresses praying within the prescribed time."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q02", "question": "How severe must the danger be for the concession?", "turns_on": "How certain and grave the threat must be.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q02/p1", "position": "A real, life-threatening inability to perform ordinary prayer is required.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba excludes suspicion; Tabari requires likelihood of death if ordinary prayer is completed. Thalabi, Qurtubi and Tabarisi describe danger obstructing full postures; Shafi'i requires visible armed enemy or a reliable warning of rapid approach."}, {"id": "2:239/q02/p2", "position": "Any feared danger that prevents the normal prayer warrants performance as possible.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says any feared circumstance permits the verse's forms; Asad specifies that standing in one place increases peril; Muqatil and others focus on inability rather than a named threat."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q03", "question": "What does rijālan mean and what is its form?", "turns_on": "Whether the term simply denotes pedestrians or specifies a moving battle group.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q03/p1", "position": "People on foot, walking or standing without mounts; a plural of rājil or rajul.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Malik gloss walking, Malik and Damghani cite 22:27. Ibn Qutayba, Zajjaj, Wahidi, Baghawi and others give analogical plural patterns; Tabari, Nahhas, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Samin list dialect plurals and cite Banu Uqayl, Banu Ghudana and pilgrimage poetry. Ibn Atiyya contrasts 2:282's ordinary men; Qaffal allows a plural of a plural."}, {"id": "2:239/q03/p2", "position": "Walkers advancing as a congregational group toward the enemy.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports this separate application, paired with mounted worshippers gesturing."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q04", "question": "How is rijālan parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q04/p1", "position": "It is an accusative circumstantial expression under an omitted command to pray or maintain prayer.", "reasons": "Farra says the condition is temporary; Tabari supplies the answer 'pray', Nahhas calls it circumstantial, and Abu Hayyan and Samin prefer supplying 'maintain the prayers' from 2:238. Tabatabai describes the omitted safe-condition antecedent."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q05", "question": "What readings of farijālan are reported?", "turns_on": "The transmitted consonants and vowels, and Tabari's preference for the widespread reading.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q05/p1", "position": "The inherited common reading is farijālan.", "reasons": "Tabari rejects two uncommon variants because they depart from widespread transmitted recitation."}, {"id": "2:239/q05/p2", "position": "Forms with rāʾ ḍamma and doubled or undoubled jīm are reported.", "reasons": "Ikrima and Abu Mujliz transmit a doubled-jim form; another Ikrima report leaves jim light. Abu Hayyan and Alusi record variants; Samin attributes forms also to Ib

{"id": "2:239/q06", "question": "What does rukbānan mean and what is its form?", "turns_on": "Whether rākib is general or technically limited to camel riders.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q06/p1", "position": "Mounted riders; a plural of rākib.", "reasons": "Tabari lists other Arabic plurals; Wahidi and Jishumi compare fāris/fursān, and Tabarisi explains the root of mounting and rikāb."}, {"id": "2:239/q06/p2", "position": "Properly a camel rider, with other mounts named separately.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaddal, al-Qaffal, al-Fadl and Samin distinguish horse rider fāris and names for donkey and mule riders; al-Fadl finds sahib plus animal more eloquent."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q07", "question": "How does aw connect the two modes, and is another reading reported?", "turns_on": "The transmitted conjunction and the force of aw.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q07/p1", "position": "The majority read aw rukbānan, joining the alternatives.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports the majority; Samin says aw can divide cases, grant permission, or offer choice."}, {"id": "2:239/q07/p2", "position": "Badīl ibn Maysara reads a second fāʾ before rukbānan.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report farijālan farukbānan."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q08", "question": "What prayer form does the fear concession permit?", "turns_on": "Whether walking combat remains prayer and how far inability can justify delaying it.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q08/p1", "position": "Pray in the feasible posture, on foot or mounted, moving if needed, using head gestures when full bowing and prostration are unsafe.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Ibrahim, Zuhri, Hasan, Jabir and numerous authorities report combat or pursuit, any heading, and gestures, with prostration lower than bowing. Wahidi retains opening takbir and recitation and travel shortening; Razi retains intention and recitation, forbids needless cries; Muqatil forbids placing forehead on anything. The Prophet's fear-prayer report via Ibn Umar distinguishes this from guarded group prayer. Abdullah ibn Unays prayed gesturing while approaching Khalid ibn Sufyan; Ibn Kathir calls the chain good."}, {"id": "2:239/q08/p2", "position": "One may pray mounted but a walker in active fighting must stop if possible or delay until safety.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and companions hold walking and fighting invalidates prayer. They cite the Prophet's delayed prayer at the Trench; some Hanafis argue rājil may mean standing on foot and combat destroys prayer form."}, {"id": "2:239/q08/p3", "position": "If even gestures are impossible, delay prayer until safe and then perform it.", "reasons": "Al-Awza'i and Makhul allow deferral under siege only when gesturing cannot be done; Tustar's fighters prayed after sunrise. Bukhari, Makhul and Awza'i defend a rare deferral using the unchallenged Tustar practice."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q09", "question": "How many units does fear prayer require?", "turns_on": "Whether fear itself shortens the prescribed count; sources also vary on fallback when two are impossible.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q09/p1", "position": "Fear leaves the normal unit count intact, or at least requires the travel count; two units are commonly specified.", "reasons": "Zuhri and Ibrahim report two; Tabari prefers the full safe count but validates one. The majority, Malik, Shafi'i and Iraqi jurists reject reduction; Jishumi argues one unit is not prayer and dawn is never shortened. Ibn Abd al-Barr doubts Bukayr's isolated one-unit report and chooses two with certainty. Tabarisi prescribes two in travel and residence except three-unit Maghrib."}, {"id": "2:239/q09/p2", "position": "One unit suffices in intense fear.", "reasons": "Qatada, Hasan, Ibn Abbas, Jabir and others report one; Ibn Abbas's formula is four at home, two in travel, one in fear. Ahmad allows it when armies engage; Ibn Kathir reports Ibn Jarir selecting one on Jabir's report. Wahidi says Ibn Abbas's school position is not acted upon."}, {"id": "2:239/q09/p3", "position": "Two units if able, one if unable.", "reasons": "Tabari transmits Qatada and Hasan's graded rule; Mujahid gives the same sequence followed by one takbir."}, {"id": "2:239/q09/p4", "position": "Two units in travel and residence except Maghrib, which remains three.", "reasons": "Tabarisi states this specific prescription."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q10", "question": "What suffices when even a full unit cannot be performed?", "turns_on": "How little outward action can still fulfill prayer under extreme inability.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q10/p1", "position": "Two takbirs or brief verbal remembrance may constitute the prayer.", "reasons": "Dahhak permits two takbirs if one unit is impossible; Said ibn Jubayr names tasbih, tahmid, tahlil and takbir during actual blows. Mujahid allows speaking as possible; Hurm ibn Hayyan called for one prostration or any gesture."}, {"id": "2:239/q10/p2", "position": "A single takbir suffices if that alone is possible.", "reasons": "Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Mujahid give this fallback; Biqai says scholars reduce extreme-fear prayer to one takbir."}, {"id": "2:239/q10/p3", "position": "Remember God inwardly when no bodily gesture is possible.", "reasons": "Thalabi transmits Zuhri's final fallback; Harali says the heart's turn to God is prayer's essence even when outward acts cannot be done."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q11", "question": "Does this concession require facing the qibla?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q11/p1", "position": "Face it when feasible; otherwise pray in any direction needed for safety.", "reasons": "Ibn Umar's report, attributed by Nafi to the Prophet, and many early authorities permit whichever direction. Wahidi explicitly says face it if possible. Razi argues continuous facing is impossible in severe danger; Qurtubi reports agreement that one may turn to save oneself."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q12", "question": "Which causes of fear qualify, including property and prohibited fighting?", "turns_on": "Whether the concession follows any serious danger or only lawful causes of danger.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q12/p1", "position": "Life-threatening enemy and nonenemy dangers generally qualify.", "reasons": "Tabari includes combat, predator, attacking camel and flood because the verse excludes no type at the requisite severity; most jurists treat enemy and other dangers alike. Razi includes defending protected lives, rebels by 49:9, fire, flood, animals and a debtor legitimately fleeing detention."}, {"id": "2:239/q12/p2", "position": "Defending property also qualifies.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this, citing the report that one killed defending property is a martyr, making the defense comparable to self-defense."}, {"id": "2:239/q12/p3", "position": "Defending property does not qualify.", "reasons": "Razi reports the opposing argument that another protected interest has greater sanctity."}, {"id": "2:239/q12/p4", "position": "Prohibited fighting does not qualify.", "reasons": "Razi says a concession would assist wrongdoing. He reports Qadi Abu al-Mahasin's nuance that self-defense is generally permitted, but obligatory against an unbeliever targeting the person."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q13", "question": "Must a completed fear prayer be repeated after safety?", "turns_on": "Whether the original act was valid, and whether enemy and nonenemy fear differ.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q13/p1", "position": "No repetition is required for an excused fear prayer.", "reasons": "Hijazi jurists say the excuse makes it valid; the Prophet's reported sword-fighting prayer need not be repeated. Another opinion waives repetition after a reliable but mistaken enemy warning."}, {"id": "2:239/q13/p2", "position": "Repeat it after safety.", "reasons": "Iraqi jurists say walking is external to prayer. Abu Hanifa requires repetition when an alleged approaching enemy departs or an apparent enemy turns out to be a dark mass."}, {"id": "2:239/q13/p3", "position": "For nonenemy danger, repeating within the time is recommended.", "reasons": "Malik distinguishes a beast or flood from enemy fighting; Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note most jurists make no such distinction."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q14", "question": "Can prayer continue across a change between fear and safety?", "turns_on": "Whether mounting and movement break continuity, and whether the direction of change matters.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q14/p1", "position": "Build on the prayer through either transition.", "reasons": "Malik, Muzani and one Shafi'i view permit completing from the first unit or after dismounting."}, {"id": "2:239/q14/p2", "position": "Restart when safety changes to fear, but build when fear changes to safety.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa draws this directional distinction."}, {"id": "2:239/q14/p3", "position": "A pedestrian may build, but a rider may not.", "reasons": "Qurtubi transmits another Shafi'i ruling."}, {"id": "2:239/q14/p4", "position": "Build in neither transition.", "reasons": "Abu Yusuf requires restarting in both cases."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q15", "question": "What role do purification and speech retain during fear prayer?", "turns_on": "Which acts remain integral and whether necessary combat or speech invalidates prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q15/p1", "position": "Purification remains required, with tayammum allowed when using water is unsafe.", "reasons": "Razi says water or earth remains available; he prefers dust even when water exists if using it threatens life, analogizing the danger to fear of thirst."}, {"id": "2:239/q15/p2", "position": "Intention and recitation remain; unrelated speech and needless cries are barred.", "reasons": "Razi states these limits despite waived standing and replacement gestures."}, {"id": "2:239/q15/p3", "

position": "Necessary action in fear may remain permissible in prayer, with speech treated like action.", "reasons": "Shafi'i infers combat does not invalidate prayer; Biqai traces Ibn Masud's greeting reports and Dhū al-Yadayn reports, discounts weak Asim against Zayd, and prefers no speech-action distinction if chronology allows; Tatimma's author, Nawawi and Subki concur."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q16", "question": "What does becoming safe mean?", "turns_on": "Whether safety is the end of imminent danger, settled residence, or any secure state.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q16/p1", "position": "The danger or fear has ended.", "reasons": "Tabari says security from enemies or other lethal threats; Muqatil specifies enemy. Tabari rejects travel return: amintum and context contrast severe fear with safety, while travel shortening remains permissible. Ibn Atiyya calls travel reading strained."}, {"id": "2:239/q16/p2", "position": "Return from travel to one's settled residence.", "reasons": "Mujahid's reading is reported by Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Durr and Alusi. Abu Hayyan adds that travel tends to be fearful and home secure; Alusi treats it as illustrative. Tabari objects that the word for settling would be iqama."}, {"id": "2:239/q16/p3", "position": "Whenever one is safe, whether before or after danger.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports this interpretation of the command; Abu Hayyan likewise reports it."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q17", "question": "What does the command to remember God require?", "turns_on": "Whether dhikr here names the restored ritual prayer, thanksgiving, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q17/p1", "position": "Resume the complete prescribed prayer.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Zayd and many later commentators identify dhikr with prayer; Tabari notes the safe prayer again has standing, bowing and prostration, and Razi cites 62:9. Damghani, Ibn Jawzi and Itqan attest dhikr for five prayers, Damghani citing 24:37. Some specify all five with full rights."}, {"id": "2:239/q17/p2", "position": "Praise and thank God for safety, divine teaching and the valid fear prayer.", "reasons": "Tabari includes praise and thanks for true guidance; Kashshaf and Ibn Atiyya cite safety and teaching of worship; Qadi objects that gratitude is also due in fear, while Razi reports that objection. Qurtubi says gratitude is for an instruction that saves a prayer from being missed."}, {"id": "2:239/q17/p3", "position": "Both prayer and gratitude.", "reasons": "Razi's third interpretation places gratitude upon safety alongside timely prayer; Abu Hayyan and Elmalili combine worship, rites and thanks."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q18", "question": "How does kamā express the relation between remembrance and God's teaching?", "turns_on": "Whether the kāf is comparative or causal and whether mā is infinitival or relative.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q18/p1", "position": "Comparison: remember or pray in the manner or measure God taught.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya distinguishes comparing thanksgiving with the gift from comparing prayer with its taught form. Abu Hayyan makes the kāf a simile and mā a verbal noun; Baydawi, Bursevi, Tabatabai and Alusi relate it to fear and safety prayer or proportional thanks. Samin calls the kāf an adjective of an omitted verbal noun or a circumstantial expression."}, {"id": "2:239/q18/p2", "position": "Cause: remember and thank God because He taught you.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls knowledge the greatest gift; Biqai says God created rescuing knowledge in people. Ibn Ashur says the causal sense follows from comparison; Burhan gives kāf among substitutes for the lām of purpose."}, {"id": "2:239/q18/p3", "position": "Mā in kamā is a verbal noun.", "reasons": "Tabarisi, Abu Hayyan and Samin parse it as infinitival; Samin prefers it. Alusi reports the option."}, {"id": "2:239/q18/p4", "position": "Mā in kamā is relative, referring to the taught prayer.", "reasons": "Samin says this permits 'pray like the prayer He taught'; Abu Hayyan attributes it to Naqqash and others, and Alusi calls it strained."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q19", "question": "How is mā lam takūnū taʿlamūn parsed and why that wording?", "turns_on": "The grammatical antecedent of mā and the rhetorical emphasis of former ignorance.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q19/p1", "position": "It is the second object of 'He taught you'.", "reasons": "Tabarisi, Qurtubi, Baydawi and Abu Hayyan identify the object. Abu Hayyan says it highlights knowledge unattainable unaided by reason."}, {"id": "2:239/q19/p2", "position": "It is an appositive of the mā in kamā.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya offers this on the prayer reading; Abu Hayyan reports it via Ibn Atiyya, and Samin reports its acceptance."}, {"id": "2:239/q19/p3", "position": "It substitutes for the omitted resumptive pronoun in allamakumūhu.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and the Shaykh prefer this; the grammarians license omitted relative pronouns, illustrated by 'the one I struck your brother' meaning 'I struck him, your brother'."}, {"id": "2:239/q19/p4", "position": "The phrase's breadth and auxiliary verb stress God's favor and prior ignorance.", "reasons": "Razi locates the ignorance before Muhammad's mission; Alusi contrasts shorter 96:5. Tabatabai says the broader wording emphasizes the scope of teaching."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q20", "question": "What did God teach that had previously been unknown?", "turns_on": "Whether the teaching is specifically prayer or the broader divine instruction.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q20/p1", "position": "Prayer and its appointed times and fear and safety forms.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Abbas on riding and walking; Wahidi specifies appointed prayer times; Kashshaf, Bursevi and others include prayer in safety and fear."}, {"id": "2:239/q20/p2", "position": "The wider religion, laws and beneficial knowledge.", "reasons": "Tabari lists lawful and forbidden things, past histories, future events and afterlife knowledge; Tabarisi adds religion and other subjects. Biqai includes this sura's rulings and subtle sciences; Harali adds bodily prayer, humility and inner secrets; Ibn Kathir names faith and welfare in both lives."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q21", "question": "How does God impart this knowledge?", "turns_on": "The theological account of divine teaching.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q21/p1", "position": "God creates knowledge in people.", "reasons": "Razi attributes this explanation to his Ashʿarite colleagues; Biqai says God graciously creates rescuing knowledge."}, {"id": "2:239/q21/p2", "position": "God furnishes proofs and acts of grace.", "reasons": "Razi attributes this to the Muʿtazila."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q22", "question": "Why are the conditions and modes worded or ordered this way?", "turns_on": "The marked order of walkers and riders and the contrast between the two conditionals.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q22/p1", "position": "Walkers come before riders as compensation for the harder form.", "reasons": "Burhan says mounted prayer is easier, so the wording advances walkers."}, {"id": "2:239/q22/p2", "position": "If presents fear as less frequent, while when presents expected security.", "reasons": "Alusi links the brief first answer and expanded second to their settings; Ibn Ashur reads the switch as a promise of victory and security."}]}
{"id": "2:239/q23", "question": "How does this verse connect with prayer commands and other fear-prayer verses?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding command or broader sequence explains the insertion and scope of this concession.", "positions": [{"id": "2:239/q23/p1", "position": "It qualifies the preceding command to preserve prayer and stand devoutly, while 4:101–103 treats related fear-prayer forms.", "reasons": "Tabarisi and Razi say the preceding full posture applies in safety; Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Kuranyolu distinguish this intense individual danger from imam-led divided-group prayer in al-Nisa.
